summary: Defines where the RIP version 2 protocol is appropriate to use within the Internet, as required by RFC 1264 before advancing it on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RIP version 2 adds routing information that version 1 cannot carry, including subnet masks and a next-hop choice. The RFC describes the kinds of networks that can use those additions while retaining RIP's simpler distance-vector approach.

questions: when should i use rip version 2
what does rip-2 add over rip-1
subtitle: Explains where RIP version 2 is useful and what its added routing fields provide.

tldr.problem: RIP version 1 cannot carry the subnet mask needed to distinguish routes when networks use variable-length subnetting, and it lacks some useful routing controls.
tldr.mechanism: RIP-2 extends RIP-1 with subnet masks, a next-hop field, authentication, and multicast advertisements.
tldr.outcome: RIP-2 can serve networks that need these features but do not require the scale or complexity of OSPF. It is not intended as a replacement for OSPF in large autonomous systems.

today: RFC 1722 is listed as an Internet Standard in the unit metadata. The metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: RIP-2 Extends RIP-1
sections.content:
This memo is an applicability statement: it explains where RIP-2 may be useful rather than defining the protocol's packet format. RIP-2 extends RIP-1; it is not a new protocol, and the operational behavior of RIP-1 remains the foundation.

The RFC says RIP-2 is not meant to replace OSPF in large or complex autonomous systems. It is intended for environments where the added features are needed but OSPF's larger, more complex link-state protocol is not required.
sections.plainLanguage: RIP-2 adds features to the existing RIP routing protocol. It is aimed at networks that need those features but can still use a simpler routing method.

sections.title: Subnet Masks Identify Routes
sections.content:
RIP-2 includes a 32-bit subnet mask after the IP address in each routing entry. This lets a router identify the exact network prefix for a route instead of guessing whether it is a network, subnet, or host route.

This matters when subnet masks have different lengths, as in variable-length subnetting and CIDR. The RFC says RIP-2 can therefore be used where routers need precise subnet-mask information but do not otherwise require OSPF.
sections.plainLanguage: A subnet mask tells a router which part of an address identifies the network. RIP-2 carries that mask with the route, so routers do not have to infer it.

sections.title: Choosing a Next Hop
sections.content:
The Next Hop field can tell a router to send traffic to a better next router rather than forwarding it through the router that advertised the route. The memo describes this as a way to remove one extra hop, including on networks where not every router runs RIP-2.

This is not a recursive route-finding method: it removes only a single extra hop. The RFC does not specify broader optimization because the risk of routing loops had not been analyzed enough.
sections.plainLanguage: A route advertisement can name a more direct next router. The feature removes one unnecessary hop, rather than searching through a chain of routers.

sections.title: Authentication and Multicast
sections.content:
Authentication is intended to stop someone who cannot directly access the network from inserting false routing information. The memo notes that the authentication mechanism in RIP-2 is limited, partly because the original RIP packet leaves only 16 octets for authentication information.

RIP-2 can send periodic advertisements using IP multicast. The RFC says this reduces load on systems that do not support RIP-2 and prevents RIP-1 routers from receiving routes whose subnet masks they would ignore.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication helps prevent unauthorized routing updates, though this format has limited space for it. Multicast announcements also keep RIP-2 routes away from RIP-1 routers that cannot interpret their masks.
